strengths: The paper tackles the well-recognized training efficiency bottleneck of 3DGS with a genuinely holistic system+algorithm codesign spanning three levels (low-level GPU kernel, mid-level data layout, high-level densification algorithm), which is a more complete treatment than most prior single-aspect acceleration works.

The warp-based rasterizer is a well-motivated and clearly explained technical contribution: reducing per-tile gradient reduction to a single warp reduction, combined with a scanline reformulation of the Gaussian exponent to cut register usage, and a hardware-aware mixed-precision/integer warp-reduce trick for covariance gradients. The microbenchmark in Table 3 convincingly isolates and quantifies this contribution against atomic, per-splat, and tensor-core baselines, showing consistent and substantial speedups.

The Cluster-Cull-Compact pipeline is a lightweight and practical adaptation of a real-time-rendering idea (Morton-code sorting + cluster-level culling/compaction) to the 3DGS training loop, and its benefit is cleanly isolated in an ablation (Table 2) showing large training-time reduction with negligible quality loss.

The opacity-gradient-variance densification metric is a reasonable statistical rationale (distinguishing unconverged-but-consistent gradients from genuinely conflicting/under-reconstructed regions) and is shown to be cheaply computable as a byproduct of the rasterizer's per-pixel statistics gathering; the paired opacity-decay mechanism is a sensible refinement over hard resets, and both components are individually ablated (Table 4).

End-to-end results are strong and span multiple operating points (turbo/balance/quality), demonstrating Pareto-optimal trade-offs against a broad and current set of baselines (3DGS, TamingGS, Mini-Splatting/v2, 3DGS-MCMC, SSS) across three standard datasets, with up to 13.4x speedup over vanilla 3DGS and competitive-to-superior PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS at greatly reduced parameter counts and training time.
The framework is reported to be open-sourced, aiding reproducibility and community adoption, which is valuable for an engineering/systems-oriented contribution of this kind.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on a single GPU (RTX 3090); claims about the generalizability of hardware-specific tricks (e.g., the integer warp-reduce accumulation trick, optimal tile size of 128, 4 pixels/thread) to 'major commercial GPUs' are asserted but not empirically validated across different architectures or vendors (e.g., newer NVIDIA generations, AMD GPUs).

Results appear to be single-run numbers with no reported variance, standard deviation, or multiple seeds, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the (sometimes modest, e.g., 0.2-0.4 dB PSNR) improvements over strong baselines like 3DGS-MCMC and SSS.

Comparisons in Table 1 mix different iteration budgets (18K/30K/40K, denoted by asterisks) across methods; while the authors partially address this by matching iterations to SSS for one setting, the overall table remains somewhat heterogeneous and could benefit from a cleaner iso-iteration or iso-time comparison for all rows.

LPIPS is occasionally worse than competing methods (e.g., LiteGS-turbo vs. Mini-Splatting/v2) despite PSNR gains, and this trade-off (attributed to fewer points capturing less high-frequency detail) is only briefly acknowledged rather than analyzed in depth (e.g., via qualitative visual comparisons or texture-detail analysis).

The paper claims a lower peak memory footprint as an advantage over aggressive densify-and-prune baselines like Mini-Splatting, but no quantitative peak-memory measurements are provided to substantiate this claim.

The three ablation studies (rasterizer, cluster-cull-compact, densification) are conducted mostly in isolation; a combined/joint ablation showing how the three levels of optimization interact (e.g., whether cluster-level locality also benefits the densification metric computation, or whether disabling one component changes the benefit of another) is not provided.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., 'Relate Work' section title typo, 'signle' typo, some inconsistent notation) suggest the manuscript would benefit from an additional proofreading pass.
